https://nineoclock.ro/medlife-launches-t.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Bucharest, July 31, 2026 – MedLife , in partnership with the Tășuleasa Social Association , announces the launch of an observational study conducted along Via Transilvanica, built around the concept of Good Stress (eustress) —a principle that is gaining increasing recognition in lifestyle medicine and longevity research. The concept suggests that controlled exposure to physical and mental challenges can activate the body’s natural adaptive mechanisms and strengthen both physical and emotional resilience. The study aims to evaluate the impact of long-distance walking on physical and emotional health in a real-world setting of sustained physical effort. It will investigate how the body responds to a multi-day walking experience in nature by analyzing biological markers alongside changes in well-being, energy levels, perceived stress, and emotional state. The study will examine, under real-life conditions, how long-distance walking influences physical health, emotional well-being, and the body’s ability to adapt to stress. The initiative builds on the findings of a recent MedLife perception study, which revealed that only one in eight Romanians regularly goes hiking, while most people continue to associate walking primarily with physical health benefits rather than its positive effects on emotional well-being. The observational study will combine objective medical measurements with qualitative research to better understand the effects of sustained walking in nature on the human body. Relevant health biomarkers will be assessed before and after participants complete their route on Via Transilvanica , while in-depth interviews will explore the emotions, motivations, and personal transformations experienced throughout the journey. All medical tests and assessments included in the MedLife study will be provided free of charge to participants, as part of an important preventive healthcare initiative. Registration opens today at www.medlife.ro/stresul-bun-via-transilvanica . The initiative is part of MedLife’s broader commitment to generating meaningful data for preventive and lifestyle medicine and is based on the findings of a recent nationwide study examining Romanians’ perceptions of physical activity. The quantitative survey, conducted by Unlock Research in May 2026 on behalf of MedLife, highlighted a clear paradox. Although Romanians acknowledge the importance of physical activity for maintaining good health, increasingly sedentary lifestyles continue to dominate. More than half of respondents (56%) reported spending most of their working day sitting, 26% said they regularly walk longer distances, while only one in eight Romanians (12%) regularly goes hiking or completes nature trails. At the same time, the study found that walking is still perceived primarily through the lens of physical health. Its benefits for emotional well-being and psychological resilience remain largely underrecognized, despite the fact that frequent hikers report higher energy levels, greater overall well-being, and a stronger ability to cope with everyday challenges. Building on these findings, MedLife is launching an observational study that combines sociological research methods with biological assessments to complement perception-based data with real-world observations. The research will examine how both the body and emotional well-being respond to sustained walking in nature. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9q.text: Figure caption, Watch: Evan Gershkovich describes the moment he was detained by masked men By Tiffany Wertheimer Published 4 hours ago US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy. In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him. "I'm not interrogated, I'm not torturedâ¦ I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game". Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal . Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false. On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story. They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place". The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service. "It's at that moment that you realise it's something really seriousâ¦ When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned." What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd. Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state. "I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years." That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap. "I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right. Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home. The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov , an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany. "They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically." Figure caption, Watch: Freed prisoners Evan Gershkovich and Paul Whelan met by Biden and Harris Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace. He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space. "That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine." Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright. "I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to." Image source, Reuters Image caption, Evan Gershkovich said he smiled at the cameras during his court appearances to show he was doing ok But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently." Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna , who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed. Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long". When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again." Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions. He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped. And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend. "I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better." Subscribe to LBC Catch Up Plus from Â£4.99 a month By Jacob Paul A British tourist is facing a wave of online backlash after complaining about the prices at the Auschwitz cafe in a scathing TikTok review.Â Lynne, who posts on TikTok under the name FreeSpirit666, has been slammed for her âpoorly judgedâ review which has since been viewed more than four million times on the social media platform.Â In the video, titled prices at Auschwitz, she complained that she and her daughter forked out Â£9 for a strawberry smoothie which tasted âvery watered downâ, and a small bottle of lemonade which tasted a âbit like Dettolâ and âtoilet cleaner â or something like that â¦ pineâ.Â She added: âVery expensiveâ¦ But the taxi from the station to here, which saved us a 25 minute walk, was Â£1.20. That was a bargain.â âSo when you come to Auschwitz, bring some food and drink, although you do get frisked at the door. We bought some â I wonder if it will go in the bin. Weâll let you know.ââ Lynn continued. Read more: BBQ restaurant blasts 'food reviewer' who offered to visit - but wanted to charge them Â£169 for the privilege Read more: Auschwitz survivor and stepsister of Anne Frank, Eva Schloss, dies aged 96 She also took aim at the lack of milk alternatives, saying: âWe fancied a coffee because we were early but they donât do decaf or any milk other than real milk â so we gave that a miss.â Her remarks have spared furious backlash online, with TikTok users flooding the comment section to criticise the review. âYou should be ashamed to even post this,â one user wrote. Many mocked her for complaining at the site of a former Nazi death camp where one of the worst human tragedies in history occurred. âIâm so sorry for your terrible experience. That must be the worst thing that has ever happened there. You poor darlings,â one commenter mocked. âThis canât be realâ¦poorly judged satire surely,â wrote another. âLetâs not forget where we are. This is a concentration camp where thousands died, not a 5 star restaurant experience,â a third added. Hitting back at the reviewer, a spokesman for the Auschwitz-Birkenau Museum said the cafe was outside the visitor services centre and operated by an external provider, with prices clearly indicated. âFor us, the essential point remains that people come to the Auschwitz Memorial to learn about the history of the German Nazi concentration and extermination camp, to confront the fate of its victims and to commemorate them,â he said. At least 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz in Poland between 1940 and 1945, the largest concentration camp operated by the Nazis during WWII.
